title_en: David Byrne Explains How Forgotten Ideas Come Back to Life
title_zh: David Byrne 谈被遗忘的好点子如何苏醒重生
subtitle_zh: 音乐人 David Byrne 携新书聊被遗忘的好点子为何沉睡、又如何被重新发现。
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 请来音乐人兼作家 David Byrne，围绕他的新书《Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up》展开对话。两位主持人先提出自己的观察：每逢金融危机、疫情等大变革时刻，就像林中开辟出一片空地，专家与外行的认知差距缩小，为新想法打开「民主化」（democratization）的市场——正如 2008 年后 Hyman Minsky 被重新发现、「Minsky 时刻」沦为陈词滥调。Byrne 解释，「Sleeping Beauty」指那些初获关注又沉入水面之下、日后被重新赏识的想法、艺术家或作品；他刻意把重点放在「如何被重新发现」而非「如何被遗忘」，因为遗忘往往是机构傲慢、种族主义、性别歧视等同一套故事，而弄清重新发现的机制，就有机会找到仍在沉睡的东西。书中案例横跨 Minsky 的复兴、Herman Melville 与《Moby Dick》、罗马混凝土里的石灰结块（lime clasts）如何被 MIT 材料科学家重新研究、巴西艺术家 Tom Zé 的再走红，以及移调与嗓音「甜蜜点」（sweet spot）等音乐话题。结尾两人畅想 AI 或成为终极的「睡美人」发现引擎——是一集关于观念如何沉睡与苏醒的跨界对谈。

turns.en: Yeah, I think there's.

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And suddenly you start to see new ways of approaching it, new entrants discussing certain things, new ideas, maybe.
turns.zh: 然后突然间，你开始看到切入问题的新方式、讨论某些话题的新入局者，也许还有新想法。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So, for example, you know, people are like, oh, the works of Hyman Minsky, for example, right? They're like, oh, maybe this guy who most people, even in economics, had not talked about very much, maybe he shed some light. We could go back and revisit him. Or even, you know, certain forms of what I would call like antique Keynesianism, et cetera. It's like, let's go back and see what people who we'd long discarded were saying. turns.zh: 比如说，你知道，大家会说，哦，Hyman Minsky 的著作，对吧？他们会说，哦，也许这个人——大多数人都没怎么谈论过他，哪怕在经济学界也是——也许他能带来一些启发。我们可以回头重新审视他。甚至是，你知道，某些我称之为老派凯恩斯主义（antique Keynesianism）之类的东西。就是说，让我们回头看看那些我们早就抛弃的人当年在说什么。也许这会是一个，也许这会有用。

turns.en: Well, Minsky is a really interesting one. Cause again, I got into financial journalism in September, 2008 and people were already bringing up the Minsky moment.
turns.zh: 嗯，Minsky 是个特别有意思的例子。因为说起来，我是 2008 年 9 月入行做财经新闻的，那时候大家就已经在提 Minsky 时刻（Minsky moment）了。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And ever since then it's become almost a cliche to the point where if I see, if I see a financial journalist talk about Minsky moment as if they just discover it, I kind of get a little annoyed and it's a little bit cringe. But what I didn't know is that basically up until 2008, a lot of Minsky's ideas had been discarded.
turns.zh: 从那以后，它几乎成了一个陈词滥调，以至于如果我看到某个财经记者谈起 Minsky 时刻，一副刚刚才发现的样子，我会有点恼火，也有点尴尬（cringe）。但我以前不知道的是，基本上直到 2008 年之前，Minsky 的很多想法都已经被抛弃了。

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.zh: 所以我们请来了一位激动人心的嘉宾，这样我们就不必一直聊下去了。我们要对话的这位，主要以重新发现 Hyman Minsky 的著作而闻名。

turns.zh: 要是我们整场对话都光聊 Minsky 也行，前提是我们也花一分钟聊聊《Moby Dick》（白鲸）。

turns.en: I knew this.
turns.zh: 我就知道。

turns.en: Was going to come up. But that's actually a legitimate example of what Sleeping Beauties is all about. Why don't, just to begin, give us the, in a nutshell, version of the book. What is a Sleeping Beauty and what are you trying to do here?

turns.en: It's not my term, but I stumbled on it. Sleeping Beauty is something that got a little bit of attention when it was first done. Could be an idea, could be a painter, could be an author. Then kind of faded from view, became kind of forgotten. Maybe not entirely, but kind of, yes, sank below the surface. And then at some point, for various reasons... got re-appreciated and came back and was like, oh yes, that is relevant right now. That's exactly what we're talking about now and this person's already done it. Let's see if there's some information, some technique, some beautiful artwork, whatever it might be for us to appreciate. You guys mentioned the, yes, 2008. Yeah. The crash, whatever you want to call it. Yeah, I have a whole section of the book on how catastrophes, including war, are kind of a way that these things get rediscovered. I decided to focus on how they got rediscovered as much as I could, rather than how they got forgotten. How they got forgotten tends to be the same stories over and over again, that institutional hubris or racism or sexism, or we think we know better than people knew in the past, all those kinds of things. But I thought, if we can find how they got rediscovered, that gives us a shot at finding the ones that are still out there, because for sure, there's some out there.
turns.zh: 这不是我发明的词，是我偶然碰上的。Sleeping Beauty 指的是那种刚出来时获得了一点关注——可能是一个想法、一位画家、一位作家——然后又渐渐淡出视野、被遗忘了的东西。也许没有完全被忘，但算是，对，沉到了水面之下。然后到了某个时点，出于种种原因……它被重新赏识、又回来了，大家会说，哦对，这东西放在当下正合适。这正是我们现在在讨论的，而这个人早就做过了。让我们看看有没有什么信息、什么技法、什么美的艺术品，随便是什么，值得我们去欣赏。你们提到了，对，2008 年。对。那场崩盘，随你怎么叫。对，我书里有一整个部分讲灾难——包括战争——如何在某种程度上成为这些东西被重新发现的途径。我尽量把重点放在它们是怎么被重新发现的，而不是怎么被遗忘的。因为被遗忘的方式往往是一遍又一遍的同样故事：机构的傲慢、种族主义、性别歧视，或者我们自以为比过去的人懂得多，诸如此类。但我想，如果我们能找到它们是如何被重新发现的，那我们就有机会找到那些至今仍在某处沉睡的东西，因为可以肯定，还有一些没被发现。

turns.en: So for the Minsky example, let's just start with that one, given our audience. But what's I think everyone knows what a Minsky moment is, but maybe talk a little bit about the time before that became a journalistic cliche, and then also talk about what's the relevance of discovering Minsky post-2008, or maybe even what the relevance would have been discovering him before 2008, other than it makes convenient anecdotes for financial columns.

turns.en: Wow. Yes. When did he do his– he did a lot of his work. I think it was in the 60s. I think that's right. Yeah. And his idea was– it's kind of behavioral economics. He was kind of saying, well, we don't exactly behave rationally. We don't always act in our best interests. I'm kind of summarizing here. Yeah. Some people already know this, that when things are flush, we tend to assume that that's the way it's always going to go. We can just pile more, you know, invest more, do this, and– And we kind of ignore the danger signs and this and that. Needless to say, he has been proven right. Yeah, he's saying we're human beings. We behave according to, with these emotional instincts, as opposed, we don't always act rationally. There was a nice story about him going on holiday with his family to Italy. How do things work here?
turns.zh: 哇。对。他是什么时候做研究的——他的很多工作，我想是在 60 年代。我记得没错。对。他的想法算是——有点像行为经济学（behavioral economics）。他大致在说，我们并不完全是理性行事的，并不总是按自己的最佳利益行动。我这里算是概括一下。对。有些人已经知道这一点：当手头宽裕、日子好过时，我们往往会假定这种好日子会一直持续下去，可以不断加码、投入更多、做这个做那个——于是我们就忽略了那些危险信号，等等等等。不用说，他已经被证明是对的。对，他在说我们是人，是凭着这些情绪化的本能行事的，而不是——我们并不总是理性行动。关于他有个很好的故事：他带家人去意大利度假，结果他没去看那些旅游景点，而是开始采访他们到访的镇子上那些做小生意的人。他想搞清楚：你们是怎么做这行的？这里的规矩是怎么运转的？

turns.en: Tracy and I can relate to that sort of thing. I think both of us, it's probably this curse of trying to learn.
turns.zh: Tracy 和我对这种事深有同感。我想我俩都是，这大概是那种拼命想搞明白一切的毛病。

turns.en: So much about the world. I don't know.
turns.zh: 想对这个世界了解得太多。我也不知道。

turns.en: Maybe you're a little bit better at turning off. No, I think we both have this curse. We go anywhere and we just try to enjoy it, but also like, how does this work? And why is the price this way? How many hours do you work? And how did you find your way into this job? So you go through in this book, Sleeping Beauty is Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, many examples, including Minsky's. including Discoveries of Roman Concrete, which we'll talk about, including the book Moby Dick itself, which we're definitely going to talk about. But before we get to that, why don't you talk to us about the process of assembling this book? Because there's thousands of Sleeping.

Or I see they're starting to fall into categories of how they got rediscovered and remembered. And I thought, okay. If I can, I need a nice little sampling in each of these categories. And then I think I'm good. I don't need to kind of overdo it. I'm not trying to be complete. I'm going to tell you every single Sleeping Beauty I've ever stumbled on. Often I'd stumble on an article about something like you said, Moby Dick or whatever. It would be something, you know, an article about Melville. And I'd say, like in one sentence, I'd go, Moby Dick was a failure and he died penniless. Something like that. And then they'd go on to talk about something else. It was like one sentence. And you guys go, whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa, you just buried the lead. From my point of view, that's the story. How did that happen? Because now, yeah, that particular, that book is revered.
turns.zh: 这样的例子太多了。对。我会把它们写下来，先写个初稿，然后，哦，这个故事不错。或者我看到它们开始按'如何被重新发现和记住'归入不同的类别。我想，好，如果我能——每一类里都需要一个不错的小样本。然后我觉得就够了，不需要做得过头。我不是想做到面面俱到，把我偶然碰到的每一个 Sleeping Beauty 都讲给你听。我常常偶然读到一篇关于某样东西的文章，就像你说的，《Moby Dick》之类的。可能是关于 Melville 的一篇文章。然后我会用一句话带过，我会说，《Moby Dick》是一部失败之作，他死时一贫如洗。诸如此类。然后他们就接着讲别的了。就一句话。而你们会说，哇哇哇哇，你这就把最劲爆的点给埋了。在我看来，那才是故事本身。那是怎么发生的？因为现在，对，那本书可是被奉为经典的。

They were friends upstate or Massachusetts, western Massachusetts, whatever. And Hawthorne said, oh, you should, maybe the next one, draw on your experiences, but maybe the next one should be more allegorical. You should get away from just the adventure yarn.
turns.zh: 你得往回倒，倒到那本书之前，这样故事才更精彩。在他开始写作之前，他签约当了一名商船水手。那时候，他们会去南太平洋和太平洋海域捕鲸、猎取各种东西。所以他干的就是这个。他觉得那是一种折磨人的、可怕至极的经历。他和另外几个人在某个岛上跳船逃了。我查过。那个岛当然美极了。你会想，我愿意住那儿。我懂。除了那些食人族之外。除了那里有食人族。对，那里有食人族。但他设法逃了出来，到了另一个岛，在那儿像个农民一样种土豆。最终他又签约上了另一条船，去了——我想是——最后到了夏威夷，结果他当初逃离的那第一条船也到了，他们说，你有罪，我们要把你带回去。你没什么办法。就像书里写的那样，他目睹了鞭刑，还有那些可怕至极的境况、可怕的虐待、发疯的船长，等等等等。我是说，书里全都有。所以他写了一本书。我想《Typee》（泰比）是第一本，讲他的南海冒险。他没说是写自己，但其实就是。然后，我想美国的出版商说，不行，这太离谱了，不可能真发生过。但我想英国有个算是目击者的人说，是的，真发生过。所有这些糟糕的事，所有这一疯狂的事都发生过。于是他们把它出版了。结果大获成功，红得发紫，成了最受欢迎的书之一。所以他又写了续集，叫——我想是——《Omoo》（欧穆），又是一个虚构的岛名，讲述了更多这类冒险。他不想再写这一类了。他有个朋友，我想是 Nathaniel Hawthorne。他们在纽约上州或者马萨诸塞州西部，反正是那一带，是朋友。Hawthorne 说，哦，你下一本也许可以取材于你的经历，但也许下一本应该更有寓言意味。你应该跳出单纯的冒险故事。

turns.en: You should still spend hundreds of words describing nautical knots.
turns.zh: 你还是应该花上几百字去描写那些航海绳结。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: But a little more fantastical. Yes.
turns.zh: 但要更奇幻一点。对。

turns.en: Yes. And so he did. Moby Dick. I think first it was called just The Whale. And it was a failure. I think, oh, in England, when it was published, I think they sold maybe 500 copies, which is not so good. He forgot, or maybe he forgot, but he didn't put the epilogue. The epilogue is where Ishmael kind of survives. Yeah. And so the English reviewers said, no, no, no. You cannot tell a story like this if everyone dies. Because who wrote it then? Who wrote it? Who's the witness? This is a rule of writing. And we didn't know this rule existed, but you can't do that. You can't have it where everyone dies because.
turns.zh: 对。所以他写了。《Moby Dick》。我想它最初就叫《The Whale》（鲸鱼）。结果它失败了。我记得，哦，在英国出版时，我想他们大概只卖出了 500 册，这可不怎么样。他忘了，也许是他忘了，没把尾声（epilogue）放进去。尾声正是 Ishmael 侥幸生还的那部分。对。所以英国的评论家们说，不行不行不行。你不能这样讲一个所有人都死了的故事。因为那这书是谁写的？谁写的？谁是那个目击证人？这是一条写作规则。我们本来不知道有这条规则，但你不能那么做。你不能让所有人都死掉，因为。

turns.en: Then- Especially if it's written in the first person.
turns.zh: 那就——尤其是如果它是用第一人称写的。

turns.en: Yes. Who's telling the story? And- Yeah, where's their information coming from? So right away, he starts getting bad reviews as well as not selling too well. And the Americans were kind of, they looked up to the British reviewers. I don't know if that still happens, but yeah, they did. And so even though he now put in the epilogue where Ishmael survives, it was too late. The bad reviews had kind of set the tone and yeah. I think he went back to Hawthorne and said, what have you done to me? I'm destroyed, which he was. He wrote other books. He wrote some weird stuff. He wrote an epic poem about the Civil War, the battles in the Civil War, kind of told from both sides. In some ways, it was kind of an anti-war, but a poem. telling stories of all the carnage and everything viewed from both sides. That did not do well. The last one that came out was one called Billy Bud. And that was discovered after his death in a bread box in the house where he lived.
turns.zh: 对。那故事是谁在讲？还有——对，他的信息是从哪来的？所以很快，他开始收到差评，销量也不好。而美国人当时有点，他们很仰仗英国的评论家。我不知道现在是不是还这样，但那时候是的。所以尽管他现在补进了 Ishmael 生还的尾声，也来不及了。那些差评已经定下了基调，就这样。我想他回去找 Hawthorne 说，你对我做了什么？我完蛋了——他确实完了。他又写了别的书。他写了些古怪的东西。他写了一部关于南北战争的史诗长诗，讲那些战役，某种程度上从双方视角来讲。在某种意义上它算是反战的，但是一首长诗，讲述双方的杀戮和种种惨状。那也没卖好。他出版的最后一本叫《Billy Budd》（比利·巴德）。那是在他去世后，在他住的那栋房子的一个面包箱里被发现的。

turns.en: That's where I keep all my unpublished manuscripts.
turns.zh: 我所有没出版的手稿就放在那儿。

turns.en: Exactly. Yeah, my bread box is just filled with manuscripts. So now he's done. He's done. I think it was... mid-1800s when he was publishing these. So kind of around the turn of the century, he's like nothing, forgotten. Someone was asked, I think, in the UK to write an article about him, and the Americans said, is he still alive? They didn't know. Anyway, so we're going back to catastrophes and wars. After World War I, People were asking themselves, how could we do this? How could we be so much killing, carnage, bloodshed? What are we made of psychologically or whatever else that allows us to do this? And his book kind of deals with that. It deals with kind of the psychology of all this stuff and it deals with kind of colonialism and racism, and all sorts of stuff that... So after World War I, people were asking, who are we? Before that, it was just kind of adventures and seafaring stories and westerns and all this kind of heroic stuff. But now it's kind of like the doubt has been put in and you go, does this book help us understand who we are?
turns.zh: 正是。对，我的面包箱里就塞满了手稿。所以到这时他已经完了。他完了。我想那大概是……19 世纪中叶他在出版这些书。所以到了世纪之交那阵，他几乎什么都不是，被遗忘了。有人被请到——我想是在英国——写一篇关于他的文章，结果美国人说，他还活着吗？他们都不知道。好了，那我们回到灾难和战争这个话题。第一次世界大战之后，人们在问自己，我们怎么能干出这种事？怎么会有这么多杀戮、惨祸、血流成河？我们在心理上或者别的方面到底是什么构成的，才让我们干得出这种事？而他的书多少就在探讨这个。它探讨这一切背后的心理，也探讨殖民主义、种族主义，还有种种……所以一战之后，人们在问，我们是谁？在那之前，人们读的都是些冒险故事、航海故事、西部故事，还有这类英雄主义的东西。但现在，怀疑的种子已经种下，你会想，这本书能帮我们理解我们是谁吗？

turns.en: I mentioned my favorite book is Moby Dick. One of my other favorite books is this book, I don't know if you've heard, Mariners, Renegades, and Castaways, the story of Herman Melville and the world we live in by the author C.L.R.
turns.zh: 我说过我最爱的书是《Moby Dick》。我另一本最爱的书是这本，不知道你听没听过，《Mariners, Renegades, and Castaways: The Story of Herman Melville and the World We Live In》（水手、叛徒与漂流者：Herman Melville 与我们身处世界的故事），作者是 C.L.R.——

turns.en: James.
turns.zh: James。

turns.en: And he talks about this a lot, that the Ahab character that Melville discovered, I mean, he created him, but arguably he discovered the character, was this character that.
turns.zh: 他大量谈到这一点：Melville 所发现的那个 Ahab 角色——我是说，他创造了这个角色，但可以说他是'发现'了这个角色——是这样一个角色，它。

turns.en: Sort of anticipated.
turns.zh: 某种程度上预见了。

turns.en: essentially the great authoritarians or the the author the authoritarians of the 20th century that when we go back and we might want to like psychoanalyze uh individuals like hitler and stalin and so forth that melville in a way saw them coming this new man sort of speak or at least it appears that way in retrospect right it appears that way this uh and this sort of um Yeah, maniacal behavior. And so the emergence of individuals later on suddenly makes Moby Dick such a compelling read.
turns.zh: 本质上预见了那些伟大的独裁者，或者说 20 世纪的那些独裁者。当我们回头看，也许会想去精神分析一下 Hitler、Stalin 这类人，而 Melville 在某种意义上预见了他们的到来——可以说是这种'新人类'，或者至少事后看起来是这样，对吧，事后看起来就是这样。这种，呃，疯狂的行为。所以后来这些人的出现，突然让《Moby Dick》成了一部如此引人入胜的作品。

turns.en: I agree. I don't know if I have anything to add there. Yeah, okay. I totally agree. It's kind of amazing that something– I don't believe that somebody like an author like that can predict the future. Sure. But I do think they kind of– They can see something in ourselves. They can see something in ourselves. They've had these– he's had these kind of really incredible experiences– and encountered kind of these really despicable people where he can incorporate that and see that this is part of who we are. And yeah, so that, yeah, later on after we've all, or everyone who was around for World War I sees kind of how low can we go, you start to go, yes, is there some way to prevent this? Can we understand ourselves so that this doesn't happen again?
turns.zh: 我同意。我不知道我还有什么可补充的。对，好。我完全同意。有点神奇的是，某种东西——我不相信像那样的一位作者能预测未来。当然。但我确实认为他们能——他们能看到我们自己身上的某种东西。他们能看到我们自己身上的某种东西。他有过这些——他有过这些真正难以置信的经历——遇到过这些真正卑劣的人，让他能够把这些融进去，看到这是我们之所以为我们的一部分。所以对，后来，当我们所有经历过一战的人都看清了人能堕落到何种地步时，你就开始想，对，有没有什么办法能阻止这种事？我们能不能理解自己，好让这种事不再发生？

turns.en: Can we talk about concrete?
turns.zh: 我们能聊聊混凝土（concrete）吗？

turns.en: Love to talk about concrete. Another odd lot. Yeah. This is something we've talked about.
turns.zh: 很乐意聊混凝土。又一个'odd lot'（冷门话题）。对。这是我们聊过的东西。

turns.en: So I have an interest in concrete, which is, you know, when I was younger and I was traveling to a lot of far-flung places, some of the most common ads and billboards that I would see in places like India or Myanmar would be for concrete brands. which you never see in the US or in Europe. People aren't advertising by this particular type of concrete. So I was always really fascinated why concrete had this position in those economies. But you point out in your book that actually the way we produce concrete nowadays, the most common way, isn't really the optimal technology for doing this. And there's actually a very ancient concrete technology that might be better in some ways. Can you describe what you found?
turns.zh: 我对混凝土有兴趣，这说来话长。我年轻的时候去过很多偏远的地方旅行，在印度或者缅甸（Myanmar）这类地方，我最常见到的广告和广告牌，有些就是混凝土品牌的——这在美国或者欧洲你是永远看不到的。那儿没人会为某个特定类型的混凝土打广告。所以我一直很好奇，为什么混凝土在那些经济体里有着这样的地位。但你在书里指出，其实我们如今生产混凝土的方式，也就是最常见的那种，并不是做这件事的最优技术。而且实际上有一种非常古老的混凝土技术，在某些方面可能更好。你能讲讲你发现了什么吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I'm going to go back to your experience because I had a similar experience. I've been to different places around the world and you see, it seems kind of incongruous. Places where sometimes the vernacular buildings in one place are kind of beautiful and then you see these concrete kind of bunker-type things, and you go, that's what was being pushed on people as being, this is what it means to be modern. One of the people mentioned in the book is from Lithuania, I think, and she said, she's from the University of Miami, and she says that, yes, when she was growing up, same thing, concrete was pushed as this will make modern housing. Right. Right. Trash chutes, clean kitchens, big windows. Oh, yeah, all the stuff. You're not going to have these little falling down wooden houses. We're going to enter the modern world. And in her words, we'll be living in the future. And so it was a big campaign to sell this stuff all around the world. It happened in the U.S. too. There was all these books about make your house out of concrete. Anyway, yeah, the story is that the Pantheon, the building in Rome, the temple in Rome, is 2,000 years old, has the largest unreinforced dome in the world, still. It doesn't have a crack in it. And it's 2,000 years old. The companies that make concrete now for parking lots and all kinds of stuff. Of course, it's reinforced with rebar. They rate it themselves to last 50 years, 5-0. 100 if we're lucky. So you've got to ask yourself, what happened? And, yes, did we just lose the recipe? Sort of, but, you know, it's a little more complicated than that. The The Romans used it a lot. These were big civic projects. They cost a lot of money. And to build the Pantheon or the Colosseum, which is also made of concrete blocks, or the aqueducts, which are made of concrete blocks, all this kind of stuff costs a lot of money, a lot of manpower. And in the course of empire, as the empire spreads out, more resources are going to kind of keep the borders intact and all that kind of stuff. And the communities on the far-flung parts of the empire, they're not so interested in using concrete. Hagia Sophia in Istanbul is made of brick and mortar. They have their own way of doing things. But So when the Roman Empire collapses, I think in 470, somewhere around there, that's it. They don't make it anymore. Nobody makes it anymore. And so it's not like the recipe got completely lost. There's this guy, Vitruvius, who wrote a book about architecture, and he includes... how to make concrete in it. I think it was in 20, boy, I'm remembering my dates. I think it was 20 BC that he did this. It was rediscovered in the Renaissance, 1400s. So that's quite a few years later. But it was considered, oh, this is an unhistorical bit of curiosity. We don't need to do that. But they liked his information about proportions. So Palladio and all these other architects in that period kind of took inspiration from him. Now I'm losing my date, but I think it's in the 1800s, a guy in England makes something called Portland cement. So we've really gone a long time. He makes something called Portland cement, starts a factory in the UK. And this is the precursor to modern concrete. It's not as good as the Roman stuff. Takes more energy to make. Puts out a lot of CO2 in the process. It doesn't last as long, but it is back and it's... It's a French guy. I forget his name. It's a French guy, maybe 30 years later. Comes up with the idea of putting rebar in to give it some tensile strength. So it's going to be better for bridges and all this kind of stuff. And yeah, so... Wow, by the 1800s, 1900s, it's being pushed as like, this is the stuff. You can build big things, bridges, highways, buildings, everything, you know, all this stuff you can build out of it. I mean, and then I can go into, I mean, what a huge energy cost this is. And of course, the stuff, as we know, doesn't last. So it's like, China does more of it than pretty much anywhere else.
turns.zh: 对，我要先回到你的经历，因为我也有过类似的经历。我去过世界各地不同的地方，你会看到，这看起来有点格格不入。有些地方的本土建筑挺美的，然后你却看到这些混凝土做的、像碉堡一样的东西，你会想，这就是当时被推销给人们、号称'这就叫现代'的东西。书里提到的一个人来自立陶宛（Lithuania），我想她是在 University of Miami（迈阿密大学）的。她说，是的，她成长的时候也一样，混凝土被推销成'这会带来现代住宅'。对。对。垃圾滑道、干净的厨房、大窗户。哦对，全套的。你不会再住那种摇摇欲坠的小木屋了。我们要进入现代世界了。用她的话说，我们将住在未来里。所以当时在全世界有一场大规模的运动来推销这东西。美国也发生了。有一堆书教你怎么用混凝土盖房子。总之，对，故事是这样的：Pantheon（万神殿），罗马的那座建筑、那座神庙，有 2000 年历史了，拥有世界上最大的无钢筋混凝土穹顶，至今仍是。它上面连一道裂缝都没有。而它有 2000 年了。如今那些为停车场之类做混凝土的公司——当然，那是用钢筋（rebar）加固的——他们自己给出的评级是能用 50 年，5-0。运气好的话 100 年。所以你不得不问自己，发生了什么？还有，对，我们是不是就把配方弄丢了？算是吧，但你知道，事情比这复杂一点。罗马人大量使用它。这些都是大型公共工程，花费巨大。建造 Pantheon，或者 Colosseum（斗兽场，也是用混凝土块建的），或者那些渡槽（aqueducts，也是混凝土块建的），所有这类东西都耗费大量金钱、大量人力。而在帝国扩张的过程中，随着疆域铺开，更多资源被投去维系边境完整之类的事情。而那些地处帝国边远地带的社群，他们对用混凝土没那么感兴趣。Istanbul（伊斯坦布尔）的 Hagia Sophia（圣索菲亚大教堂）就是用砖和砂浆建的。他们有自己的做法。所以当罗马帝国崩溃时——我想是在 470 年前后，大概那个时候——就到此为止了。他们不再生产它了。没人再生产了。所以并不是说配方彻底失传了。有个人叫 Vitruvius（维特鲁威），他写了一本关于建筑的书，里面就收录了……如何制作混凝土。我想那是在 20 年——天哪，我在回忆我的年份——我想是公元前 20 年他写的。它在文艺复兴时期、也就是 15 世纪 40 年代被重新发现。所以那已经是相当多年以后了。但当时人们觉得，哦，这是一件与历史无关的稀奇玩意儿，我们用不着那个。不过他们喜欢他关于比例的信息。所以 Palladio（帕拉第奥）以及那个时期的其他建筑师都从他那里汲取灵感。现在我又记不清年份了，但我想是在 19 世纪（1800s），英国有个人做出了一种叫 Portland cement（波特兰水泥）的东西。所以我们已经走了很长一段路了。他做出这种叫波特兰水泥的东西，在英国开了一家工厂。这就是现代混凝土的前身。它不如罗马的东西好，制作起来更耗能，过程中排放大量 CO2，也没那么耐久，但它确实回来了，而且……是这么个法国人。我忘了他名字。是个法国人，大概 30 年后，想出了往里加钢筋的主意，好给它一些抗拉强度。这样它就更适合建桥之类的东西了。所以对……哇，到了 19 世纪、20 世纪，它被大肆推销成'就是这个东西'。你能用它建大型工程——桥梁、公路、建筑，什么都能建，你知道，所有这些东西都能用它来建。我是说，然后我还可以讲讲，这是多么巨大的能源开销。当然，正如我们所知，这东西并不耐久。所以就像，中国用得比几乎任何地方都多。

turns.en: But the guy who invented Portland cement, was he just unaware of the Roman recipe? Or was he maybe thinking about other things like, you know, it's cheaper to build. We don't have to get special ash from Mount Vesuvius or whatever it is. Did he have other considerations?
turns.zh: 但发明 Portland cement 的那个人，他是压根不知道罗马的配方吗？还是说他也许在考虑别的东西，比如，你知道，这样建更便宜，我们不必去 Mount Vesuvius（维苏威火山）弄什么特殊的火山灰之类的。他有没有别的考量？

turns.en: Yeah, there was a thought that... They'd look at the Roman recipe and think, oh, it's special because they used the ash from Vesuvius. They got the secret sauce, and we don't have that. So we have to do with what we have. They also saw the Roman stuff. This is going to lead to the solution. The Roman stuff has all these little white specks in it, and I thought, They just didn't know how to mix it well. They didn't have the mixing technology. We can do that. So yeah, we're okay.
turns.zh: 对，当时有种想法是……他们看着罗马的配方，会想，哦，它之所以特别，是因为他们用了维苏威火山的灰。他们有那个'独门秘方'，而我们没有。所以我们只能用手头的材料将就。他们还看到罗马的东西……这会引出解决办法。罗马的混凝土里全是一个个小白点，我就想，他们只是不懂得怎么把它搅匀罢了。他们没有那个搅拌技术。我们能做到。所以对，我们没问题。

turns.en: So ours is better, basically, aesthetically at least.
turns.zh: 所以我们的基本上更好，至少外观上是。

turns.en: It's kind of a bias, prejudice, whatever that we have, that whatever we know is better and smarter than whoever went before. That's just another kind of... An example of how irrational we can be. But it was these little specks, they're called lime karsts, that there was some material scientists at MIT who started looking into it about 15 years ago or so. And they did a test where they had the Roman stuff and they had some contemporary stuff and they poured water on it. And the water eventually went through the contemporary stuff.
turns.zh: 这算是我们的某种偏见、成见，随便你怎么叫——总觉得我们懂的比前人都更好、更聪明。这只是又一个……说明我们能有多不理性的例子。但正是这些小白点，它们叫石灰结块（lime clasts），大约 15 年前，MIT（麻省理工）的一些材料科学家开始研究它。他们做了个实验：他们拿了罗马的材料，又拿了些当代的材料，往上面浇水。结果水最终渗过了当代的材料。

turns.en: Which leads to cracks, right?
turns.zh: 那就会导致裂缝，对吧？

turns.en: Which leads to cracks, yes. Especially if it gets cold. But even if it doesn't. And then with the Roman stuff, it goes in and some of this lime car stuff, these little white specks dissolve and the cracks heal up. It's self-healing. But the other stuff, especially if it's got rebar in it, the water gets in. If it hits the rebar, the rebar is going to rust and crack and kind of expand, the rusting rods expand and make more cracks. So 2023, the folks at MIT started a company, and they've started to make the Roman stuff. Whether the world kind of beats a path to their door, it remains to be seen, but it has been rediscovered.
turns.zh: 那就会导致裂缝，对。尤其是如果天气变冷的话。但即使不冷也会。而对于罗马的材料，水渗进去后，一些这种石灰结块、这些小白点会溶解，然后裂缝就愈合了。它是自愈的（self-healing）。但另一种材料，尤其是如果里面有钢筋，水渗进去，一旦碰到钢筋，钢筋就会生锈、开裂并膨胀，生锈的钢筋膨胀又会造成更多裂缝。所以到了 2023 年，MIT 的那帮人成立了一家公司，开始生产罗马那种混凝土。至于全世界会不会纷纷找上门来，还有待观察，但它确实被重新发现了。

turns.en: I would have loved to hear the initial conversation that's like, what do you want to study at MIT? And it's, I really want to look into those little, you know, like discolorations on Roman cement.
turns.zh: 我真想听听他们最初的那段对话，比如，'你在 MIT 想研究什么？'答案是，'我真的特别想研究罗马水泥上那些小小的，你知道，那些变色的小斑点。'

turns.en: That's the cool thing about universities.
turns.zh: 这正是大学了不起的地方。

turns.en: People can just have the time and space to find niche things. I'm curious, you know, obviously you have been a famous, successful artist, musician for a very long time. Recently, or back in 2023, A24 re-released the 1984 Talking Heads concert film Stop Making Sense, sort of re-energizing, maybe introducing a new generation of listeners to the Talking Heads and so forth.
turns.zh: 人们可以有时间和空间去钻研那些冷门的东西。我很好奇，你知道，显然你作为一位著名的、成功的艺术家、音乐人已经很多年了。最近，或者说回到 2023 年，A24 重新发行了 1984 年那部 Talking Heads 的演唱会电影《Stop Making Sense》，算是重新点燃了热情，也许把新一代的听众介绍给了 Talking Heads 等等。

turns.en: Is that a Sleeping Beauty? Is that like... I mean.
turns.zh: 那算是一个 Sleeping Beauty 吗？那算不像……我是说。

turns.en: there was no period in which there weren't people listening to the talking heads, but perhaps like there was like, at least among some people, some like re-spark of interest.
turns.zh: 从来没有哪个时期是没人听 Talking Heads 的，但也许，至少在一部分人当中，重新燃起了一些兴趣。

turns.en: It's definitely been that. It's definitely been increased interest.
turns.zh: 确实是这样。确实是有更多兴趣了。

turns.en: What's been your experience of, okay, something happens. Someone says, you know what? This 1984 concert film, maybe it would be relevant again. Maybe there's people who would appreciate it again. What's been your experience with at least one specific cultural artifact of yours sort of gathering new life basically 40 years later?
turns.zh: 你的体验是怎样的？就是说，好，某件事发生了。有人说，你知道吗？这部 1984 年的演唱会电影，也许它会重新变得有意义，也许有人会重新欣赏它。当你的至少一件具体的文化作品在差不多 40 年后重新焕发新生时，你的体验是怎样的？

turns.en: I've been doing the whatever, the music thing. The music thing. The music thing long enough that I've seen my career go up and down. Um, in the nineties, uh, might've been the music I was doing. It might've been whatever, but my career went down. I was back to playing little clubs in lots of places where I'd been playing much larger venues. Now I'm back to playing these sizable places again. That feels, yes. And I thought, but it's, but in some cases I'm playing the same stuff. Yeah. I didn't change. I mean, I had gotten older. but it's all these other, it's all the context. The audience, the demographic, another generation, whatever it might be, those things have changed. Just like a lot of the things in this book, the paintings of Botticelli or whatever haven't changed, but they go in and out of fashion. And I realized, oh yeah, I've experienced that. How does that feel? How does it feel to go out of fashion for time? It must suck.
turns.zh: 我做这个，做音乐这行，做音乐这行，做音乐这行已经够久了，久到我见证过自己事业的起起落落。嗯，在 90 年代，呃，也许是我当时做的音乐，也许是别的什么原因，但我的事业走下坡了。我又回到在很多地方的小俱乐部演出，而那些地方我曾经是在更大的场地演的。现在我又重新回到这些相当大的场地演出了。那种感觉，对。我想，但，但在某些情况下我演的是同样的东西。对。我没变。我是说，我确实变老了，但都是这些其他的，全都是语境变了。观众、人群构成、又一代人，不管是什么，这些东西变了。就像这本书里的很多东西一样，Botticelli（波提切利）的画作之类的并没有变，但它们会一时流行、一时过气。我意识到，哦对，我经历过那个。那是什么感觉？一时过气是什么感觉？那肯定很糟。

turns.en: Does it get more comfortable when there's another wave? You're like, I've been here before. This isn't as painful. I know that this is a pendulum. I'm very curious about this.
turns.zh: 当又一波浪潮来临时，会不会更从容一些？你会想，我以前经历过。这次没那么痛苦了。我知道这是个钟摆。我对此非常好奇。

turns.en: Oh, yeah. After it's happened once, if something happens like that again, you go, yes, I know. Don't take this personally. Don't take it personally. The work might be good. You may have done something terrible or Not so good, but don't assume that it's because the work is bad. Yeah. But I remember at the time, I just felt like, no, you just have to slog on. Just kind of keep going. Obviously, you can only keep going like that for a while until, and if things go lower, you go, I have no income. But to some extent, yeah, I think you just have.
turns.zh: 哦，对。当这种事发生过一次以后，如果再来一次同样的事，你会想，对，我懂。别往心里去。别往心里去。作品可能是好的。你可能做了件糟糕的、或者不那么好的东西，但别假定那是因为你作品差。对。但我记得当时，我就是觉得，不，你只能咬牙硬撑下去，就是继续做下去。显然，你只能这样撑一阵子，直到——如果情况更糟，你会想，我没有收入了。但在某种程度上，对，我觉得你只能。

turns.en: To, How do you tell the difference between, oh, I was unlucky or the audience wasn't ready for this or the audience doesn't appreciate how special this is versus I have failed to create something that resonates with my audience? Because I'm sure everyone has experienced this in their professional or creative lives at one point or another. If you do something or you make something and it doesn't get the result that you want or the reception that you want, the temptation is to, you know, just kind of blame it on something else or excuse it away. You know, it's not that I'm out of touch. It's the children who are wrong, that sort of thing. So how do you balance those two things?
turns.zh: 说到，你怎么区分——哦，是我运气不好，或者观众还没准备好接受这个，或者观众不懂得欣赏这东西有多特别——和'我没能创造出能与观众产生共鸣的东西'这两者？因为我相信每个人在自己的职业或创作生涯中，都多少经历过这个。如果你做了某件事、或造出某个东西，结果没有得到你想要的成果或你想要的反响，那种诱惑就是，你知道，把它归咎于别的什么、或者找借口开脱。你知道，'不是我跟不上时代，是这些孩子错了'，诸如此类。所以你如何在这两者之间取得平衡？

turns.en: I realize it's a little bit of both. In that period, I did a couple records where I worked with Latin musicians and I was doing all Latin rhythms and all all that. I was having a great time. It went down really well in Latin America and in parts of Europe. But in the U.S. in particular, it was like, no, you've betrayed us. This is not what we want from you. And I realized, oh, okay. I get that. I can maybe, I probably thought, I can maybe temper this somehow. Yeah, I do understand that, yeah, if you Completely betray what your audience is expecting or hoping for. Yeah, that's not going to work for it. But there's a way to still do something interesting, something exciting, and acknowledge a little bit what they're hoping for. And I thought, okay, I can kind of self-correct a little bit.
turns.zh: 我意识到这多少是两方面都有。在那段时期，我做了几张唱片，跟拉丁音乐人合作，全是拉丁节奏之类的。我玩得很开心。它在拉丁美洲和欧洲部分地区反响非常好。但在美国，尤其是，那感觉就像，不，你背叛了我们。这不是我们想从你这儿听到的。我意识到，哦，好吧。我懂那个。我也许，我当时大概想，我也许可以在某种程度上调和一下这个。对，我确实理解，对，如果你完全背叛了观众的期待或指望，对，那行不通。但有一种方式，仍然能做出有意思的、令人兴奋的东西，同时又在一定程度上回应他们所期待的。我就想，好，我可以在某种程度上自我修正一下。

turns.en: Speaking of your interest in Latin American music, you tell a story about, and I think it's actually the first chapter of the book, the Brazilian artist Tom Zay. And you went down to Brazil and you tell a story of someone getting a big stack of records and the cover of this one record was a little different. You checked it out and it was amazing, but it was an artist that not many people had been familiar with. You repopularized him from your label. But rather than just talk about that per se, I want to ask, like, you know, something that I've observed that has really changed in my lifetime is that it used to be that anything that was sort of avant-garde, whether it was music, whether it was political ideas, etc., it used to be really hard to find. Like, it used to be that, like, if you wanted to read sort of heterodox political philosophy, you had to go to obscure bookstores or When I was younger, if I wanted to seek out a sort of indie music of some sorts, I used to literally write letters to record labels and then they would like send back the catalogs. This was like in the early nineties, et cetera. The thing that's changed is that very mainstream musicians are in very avant-garde musicians are both just a one click away. Now you just type in a different name on Spotify, et cetera. And so the digitization process of everything. removes that sort of physical link that used to exist between sort of like you really had to put in work to find the avant-garde thing before. Physical work, in many cases. Go to a location, go to Brazil, et cetera.
turns.zh: 说到你对拉丁美洲音乐的兴趣，你讲了一个故事，我想那其实是书里的第一章，讲巴西艺术家 Tom Zé（汤姆·泽）。你去了巴西，讲了一个故事：有人拿来一大摞唱片，其中一张的封面有点不一样。你看了看，觉得它太棒了，但那是一位没多少人熟悉的艺术家。你通过你的厂牌让他重新走红。不过，与其就事论事地谈这个，我想问的是，你知道，有件事是我这辈子观察到、并且真的改变了的：过去，任何前卫（avant-garde）的东西，不管是音乐、还是政治思想等等，过去都很难找到。就是说，过去如果你想读那种非主流的政治哲学，你得去那些冷门的书店；或者我年轻的时候，如果想找某种独立音乐，我真的会给唱片公司写信，然后他们就把目录寄回来。那大概是 90 年代初，等等。而改变的是：如今，非常主流的音乐人和非常前卫的音乐人，都只是一键之遥。你现在只要在 Spotify 上输入一个不同的名字就行了，等等。所以这一切的数字化过程，移除了那种过去存在的实体纽带——你以前真的得下功夫才能找到那个前卫的东西。实体上的功夫，很多情况下。得跑到某个地方去，跑到巴西去，等等。

turns.en: Now you don't.
turns.zh: 现在你不用了。

turns.en: How does that change the sort of discovery of the sleeping beauties when the sort of physical constraints are no longer there? Everything is just a search away.
turns.zh: 当那些实体上的限制不复存在时，这如何改变了发现这些 sleeping beauties 的方式？一切都只是一次搜索之遥。

turns.en: I'm going to agree and also push back on some of that. I think not everything is on streaming or on the internet. I remember hearing a talk, I think, from Bob Woodward or someone. We were talking about some research he was doing from a book. And he realized that there was something in somebody's basement. And they had boxes full of files. And it was physical stuff. I mean, the internet was there, but Those things just weren't on it. And he had to go and go to this person's basement. And I thought, yeah, there's still stuff that's kind of hidden from view. But that said, I definitely agree that with streaming music, to some extent with films and other kinds of information, I know especially with music, a whole... If they're interested in something that's old, they can just listen to it. And if they like it, add it to their playlist. So they end up, I think, sometimes with playlists that mix all these different genres. They come from different decades, different eras, which is kind of great. They're just putting it in there because they like it, not because, oh, this is the cool thing that's happening right this minute. at this moment, on these services, there's very little information. I mean, you can dig and get the information, but what's.
turns.zh: 我既要同意，也要反驳其中一些。我认为并不是所有东西都在流媒体或互联网上。我记得听过一次演讲，我想是 Bob Woodward（鲍勃·伍德沃德）或者谁的。我们在谈他为某本书做的一些研究。他意识到，有个东西在某人的地下室里。他们有一箱箱的文件。那是实体的东西。我是说，互联网是有的，但那些东西就是不在上面。他不得不亲自跑去这个人的地下室。我就想，对，仍然有些东西是藏在视野之外的。话虽如此，我确实同意，随着流媒体音乐——在某种程度上还有电影和其他类型的信息——我尤其在音乐方面知道，一整个……如果他们对某个老东西感兴趣，他们直接就能听。如果喜欢，就加进自己的播放列表。所以我觉得，他们最后有时候会有那种混合了各种不同流派的播放列表。它们来自不同的十年、不同的年代，这其实挺棒的。他们把东西放进去，纯粹是因为喜欢，而不是因为，哦，这是此时此刻、这个当口最酷的东西。而在这些服务上，信息非常少。我是说，你可以去挖、去找到那些信息，但是那个……

turns.en: But the liner notes used to be a really fun part of.
turns.zh: 但唱片内页说明（liner notes）以前真的是……很有意思的一部分。

turns.en: Buying a record. Yeah, and you know, like, oh, this is produced by so-and-so, and this is who wrote it.
turns.zh: 买唱片时的一部分。对，而且你知道，就像，哦，这张是谁谁制作的，这首是谁写的。

turns.en: Looking at the art and stuff. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 看那些封面美术之类的。对对对。

turns.en: So there's very little of that, which I miss some of that, but it also has the advantage of when you don't know Then you're not kind of put off by any of those factors, like when it was done, the dates or whatever. You're just listening kind of blind and going, I like that. I don't know how it was received at the time, where it fits in. It's kind of, a lot of the context is kind of removed.
turns.zh: 所以现在这方面信息很少，这我也挺怀念其中一些的，但它也有个好处：当你不了解时，你就不会被任何那些因素劝退，比如它是什么时候做的、年代之类的。你就是有点'盲听'，然后想，我喜欢那个。我不知道它当时反响如何，不知道它处在什么位置。某种程度上，很多语境都被剥离掉了。

turns.en: Conversely, though, the fact that all this information and cultural content is now available on the internet or on streaming services means that in some ways discovery also gets harder. There's an information overload, I guess, like a curation problem. So for instance, I went to LA recently. I went to a random tiki bar out in the suburbs and they had on a haunted surf tiki playlist, which was a genre that I never knew existed. But apparently there are a lot of, you know, sort of like, halloweeny surf songs out there um i never would have thought to put that in the search engine bar on spotify there's a playlist there but i would not have gone looking for it i would have been listening to any of the like hundreds of other songs that the algorithm was recommending to me today when we're sort of overwhelmed by both informational and content choices why does that mean for the rediscovery of old ideas?
turns.zh: 不过反过来说，如今所有这些信息和文化内容都能在互联网或流媒体服务上获得，这意味着在某些方面，发现也变得更难了。存在一种信息过载，我想，也就是一个策展（curation）的问题。比如说，我最近去了 LA（洛杉矶）。我去了郊区一家随便撞见的 tiki 酒吧，他们放着一个'闹鬼冲浪 tiki'（haunted surf tiki）的播放列表，那是一个我从不知道存在的流派。但显然外面有很多那种，你知道，有点万圣节味儿的冲浪歌曲。我永远都不会想到要在 Spotify 的搜索栏里输入那个。那儿是有一个这样的播放列表，但我本来是不会去找它的，我本来会去听算法那天推荐给我的其他几百首歌里的任意一首。所以当我们被信息和内容选择同时淹没时，这对重新发现旧想法又意味着什么？

turns.en: You're absolutely right. When there's so much out there, as I was doing some of this research, I saw that Condoleezza Rice said that part of the problem with the Challenger explosion was a filter problem. The information and the warning about the O-rings and all this stuff was out there. It wasn't like nobody knew. It was out there. But when there's so much information, it doesn't like jump out and say, over here, take a look at this. Yeah, you can miss things even if they're still there.
turns.zh: 你说得完全对。当外面的东西太多时，我在做一些这方面研究的时候看到，Condoleezza Rice（康多莉扎·赖斯）说过，挑战者号（Challenger）爆炸的部分问题是一个'过滤'（filter）的问题。关于那些 O 形密封圈（O-rings）的信息和警告，都在那儿。并不是说没人知道。它就在那儿。但当信息太多时，它就不会跳出来对你说，'在这儿，来看看这个'。对，即使那些东西还在那儿，你也可能错过它们。

turns.en: Can I ask a question from one musician to another?
turns.zh: 我能以一个音乐人的身份，问另一个音乐人一个问题吗？

turns.en: I have a band.
turns.zh: 我有个乐队。

turns.en: We play country music. This is just a pure music question, actually. It has nothing to do with discovery things.
turns.zh: 我们演奏乡村音乐（country music）。其实这纯粹是个音乐问题。跟'发现'那些事儿没关系。

turns.en: Any particular kind of country music?
turns.zh: 某种特定类型的乡村音乐吗？

turns.en: No, I would say it's kind of like down the middle country, maybe a little bit classic, et cetera. But I'm like a very bad guitarist, so I write all my songs in G or C because those are easy chords for me to play. Is there any difference between scales? So it's like if I write a song in G major and then someone else plays the song, it's like I could have written it in C major or A major. These are all easy chords to play. In your experience, is there a difference? Does something change when you transpose a song into a different scale?
turns.zh: 不，我会说它算是那种居中路线的乡村音乐，也许有点老派（classic），等等。但我吉他弹得很差，所以我所有的歌都用 G 调或 C 调来写，因为那些和弦对我来说好弹。不同调式之间有区别吗？就是说，如果我用 G 大调写了一首歌，然后别人来演奏它，就像我本来也可以用 C 大调或 A 大调来写。这些都是好弹的和弦。以你的经验，有区别吗？当你把一首歌移调（transpose）到不同的调式时，会有什么变化吗？

turns.en: I only realized kind of recently that, yeah, you can transpose a song into it when I'm in the writing process. You can move it into another key and try it a little higher, try it a little lower, try it at different places. And eventually you hit one and you go, oh, that's the sweet spot for my voice. For your voice. For my voice. But is the song the same? That's a good question. I know that sometimes, especially on guitar, you're saying like a G chord, it has a lot of open strings in it. So you hit it and it just rings out. Whereas if you're playing, I don't know, a B flat or whatever, doesn't ring out the same way. You might have to put a capo, a thing, to adjust kind of where the neck of the guitar hits and all this kind of thing to get that kind of effect. You might be able to recreate that effect. But yeah, the guitar itself sounds different, which gives a kind of different feeling depending on what key you're playing it in. The way the notes are stacked on a guitar or on a piano, Yeah. Probably has a different feeling too. But, well, the good news for me was you can, which I thought, why didn't I know this earlier? You can move stuff until it hits kind of the sweet spot for your voice.
turns.zh: 我也是最近才意识到，对，你可以把一首歌移调——当我处在创作过程中时。你可以把它挪到另一个调里，试试高一点，试试低一点，试试不同的位置。最终你会碰到某一个，然后你会想，哦，那正是适合我嗓音的甜蜜点（sweet spot）。适合你的嗓音。适合我的嗓音。但歌还是同一首吗？这是个好问题。我知道有时候，尤其是在吉他上，你比如说一个 G 和弦，它里面有很多空弦（open strings）。所以你一弹，它就那么鸣响出来。而如果你弹的是，我不知道，一个降 B（B flat）或者别的什么，它就不会以同样的方式鸣响。你可能得放一个变调夹（capo），一个小装置，来调整吉他琴颈按弦的位置之类的，才能得到那种效果。你也许能重现那种效果。但是的，吉他本身听起来就不一样，这会根据你用哪个调来弹，带出一种不同的感觉。音符在吉他上或者钢琴上排列堆叠的方式，对，大概也会带来不同的感觉。不过，对我来说的好消息是你可以——我当时想，为什么我没早点知道这个？——你可以把东西挪来挪去，直到它落到适合你嗓音的那个甜蜜点上。

turns.en: I don't have a music question.
turns.zh: 我没有音乐方面的问题。

turns.en: I'm sorry.
turns.zh: 抱歉。

turns.en: But maybe it relates to musicians. What's the cost of not recognizing good ideas, good songs contemporaneously? So, okay. Maybe Joe isn't recognized in his own time as a great country music singer, and we don't get good country songs from Joe or more good country songs from Joe. Maybe in the example of concrete, if we had been using the Roman recipe before, we would have had longer-lasting buildings, less energy expenditure, less global warming, things like that. Talk to us about the cost of not recognizing these things in their own time.
turns.zh: 不过它也许跟音乐人有关。在同一个时代没能识别出好想法、好歌曲，代价是什么？就是说，好吧，也许 Joe 在他自己的时代没被认可为一位伟大的乡村音乐歌手，于是我们就听不到 Joe 的好乡村歌曲，或者听不到 Joe 更多的好乡村歌曲。也许拿混凝土来说，如果我们之前就用罗马的配方，我们本可以有更耐久的建筑、更少的能源消耗、更少的全球变暖，诸如此类。跟我们谈谈，在当时那个时代没能识别出这些东西，代价是什么。

turns.en: It's a little hard to... to talk about the cost of, say, not recognizing musicians or composers or painters or things like that. I think it's real. That cost is real. But it's hard to measure. The kind of pleasure and joy and satisfaction you get from something like that and what it means for you, maybe giving you insights and psychological and other kinds of benefits you get to it, it's kind of hard to measure. So that kind of gets... maybe pushed aside and disregarded to some extent. Whereas, as you said, something like concrete or the medical things, like there's a story on hand washing where people are dying and all they need to do is for the doctors to wash their hands. And yeah, so you realize, no, in many cases, it's very measurable. These lives could have been saved these buildings could have been less energy intensive and they could have lasted longer. That's pretty easy to measure.
turns.zh: 这有点难……谈论，比如说，没能识别出音乐家、作曲家、画家或类似这些东西的代价。我认为它是真实存在的。那种代价是真实的。但它很难衡量。你从这样的东西里得到的那种愉悦、快乐和满足，以及它对你意味着什么——也许给了你洞见，还有你从中获得的心理上和其他方面的好处——它很难衡量。所以那种东西多少会被……被推到一边、在某种程度上被忽视。而正如你说的，像混凝土这样的东西，或者医学上的东西——比如有个关于洗手的故事：人们在死去，而他们所需要做的，就是让医生去洗手。对，所以你会意识到，不，在很多情况下，这是非常可衡量的。这些生命本可以被挽救，这些建筑本可以更省能源、更耐久。那是相当容易衡量的。

turns.en: One way that new ideas, old ideas can be rediscovered and then applied is I think by an individual being sort of aggressively pluralistic about what they consume.
turns.zh: 我认为，新想法、旧想法被重新发现进而被应用的一种途径，是让一个人在自己所'消费'的内容上保持一种积极的多元主义（aggressively pluralistic）。

turns.en: So like read a lot of books that aren't necessarily in your beat.
turns.zh: 就是说，多读一些不一定在你报道领域（beat）之内的书。

turns.en: We cover markets, finance, and economics, but I think we would be worse at it if we only read books about markets, finance, and economics. On the other hand, and maybe this is just me, and maybe this is just the curse of how my brain works. I have this tendency to like read anything and I'm like, oh, that's really applicable right now.
turns.zh: 我们报道市场、金融和经济，但我想如果我们只读关于市场、金融和经济的书，我们反而会做得更差。另一方面，也许这只是我个人的毛病，也许这只是我大脑运作方式的诅咒。我有一种倾向，就是随便读点什么，然后就会想，哦，这个放在当下真是太适用了。

turns.en: And then I'll read the next book. It's like, oh, amazing.
turns.zh: 然后我读下一本书。就会想，哦，太棒了。

turns.en: That's really applicable right now. And then I'll read the next book. It's like, wow, the lessons of this book. That's just sounds like what's happening right now. And our brains can actually are very good at over-metaphorizing, maybe, examples. So, like, I don't know if that's a word, but it's tempting to, like, look at anything and say, wow.
turns.zh: 这个放在当下真是太适用了。然后我读下一本书。就会想，哇，这本书的教训。那听起来就跟当下正在发生的一模一样。而我们的大脑其实非常擅长过度比喻化（over-metaphorizing），也许是，那些例子。所以，我不知道这是不是一个词，但那种诱惑就是，随便看什么都会说，哇。

turns.en: That's like- How do we avoid sleeping uglies?
turns.zh: 那就像——我们要怎么避免'sleeping uglies'（沉睡的丑东西）呢？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: How do you avoid this sort of- find every new thing you come across to say, wow, we should all be talking about that again. Because our brains are so good at maybe coming up with a tortured reason why. this idea of old is actually very relevant to now.
turns.zh: 你要怎么避免这种——每碰到一个新东西就说，哇，我们都应该重新谈论它。因为我们的大脑太擅长也许编造出一个牵强的理由，来说明为什么这个古老的想法其实跟当下非常相关。

turns.en: I have to say, I do the same thing, and I think it's pretty good.
turns.zh: 我得说，我也干同样的事，而且我觉得这挺好的。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: There's a story in here about a woman, a scientist, Lynn Margulis, who basically ended up, she proposed, and it was later confirmed and proven, that the cells in our bodies, the cells in plants, are the result of a symbiotic merging between an early kind of organism and bacteria. The bacteria became the mitochondria that do provide the energy from oxygen or from sunlight or whatever and whatever. So this evolutionary big, big, big step millions of years ago came as a result of a kind of symbiotic cooperation. And so I immediately go, aha, cooperation is key. And there's another story about this Russian evolutionary anarchist philosopher guy, Kropotkin, who also says, sometimes cooperation is a better strategy than competition. Not always, but sometimes. And of course, I thought, okay, wow, that is a kind of metaphor that I can just cut and paste all over the place and see where it fits.
turns.zh: 这里面有个故事，讲一位女性、一位科学家，Lynn Margulis（琳·马古利斯）。她基本上最终——她提出了一个假说，后来被证实、被证明了——就是说，我们身体里的细胞、植物里的细胞，是一种早期生物与细菌之间共生融合（symbiotic merging）的结果。那些细菌变成了线粒体（mitochondria），正是它们从氧气、或者从阳光之类的东西中提供能量，不管是什么。所以这个几百万年前进化上的巨大、巨大、巨大的一步，是某种共生合作的结果。于是我立刻就想，啊哈，合作是关键。还有另一个故事，讲这位俄国的进化论无政府主义哲学家，Kropotkin（克鲁泡特金），他也说，有时候合作是比竞争更好的策略。不是永远，但有时候。我当然就想，好，哇，这是一个我可以到处剪贴、看它适合哪儿就贴哪儿的比喻。

turns.en: I like the lichen guy who very early on caught on to the idea that lichens were an amalgamation of, I guess, fungi and algae. And no one believed him to the extent that his name became an insult in the academic community. What was his name again? It started with like an S or something.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个研究地衣的人，他很早就领会到，地衣（lichens）是一种——我想是——真菌（fungi）和藻类（algae）的结合体。而没人相信他，以至于他的名字在学术界都成了一句骂人的话。他叫什么来着？好像是 S 开头的什么的。

turns.en: I can't remember.
turns.zh: 我想不起来了。

turns.en: It sounded like a good insult, but I mean, poor guy, because he was directionally correct.
turns.zh: 那听起来是句挺好用的骂人话，但我是说，可怜的家伙，因为他的方向是对的。

turns.en: Schwarzkopf or something like that. Yes. Yeah, I can't remember the exact name, but yes, he's proved right. That's interesting to say.
turns.zh: Schwarzkopf（施瓦茨科普夫）之类的。对。是啊，我记不清确切的名字了，但是的，他被证明是对的。这么说还挺有意思的。

turns.en: I'm currently, because AI is like everything right now, so I'm trying to learn a little bit more about that.
turns.zh: 我最近，因为 AI 如今几乎就是一切，所以我在试着多了解一点这方面的东西。

turns.en: I'm reading this interesting book. It's called What is Intelligence? It came about a year ago.
turns.zh: 我在读一本很有意思的书。它叫《What is Intelligence?》（什么是智能）。大概一年前出的。

turns.en: And he says the exact same thing, that actually evolution is co-evolution, that if you look at the history of things, that basically the way the world emerges is there's thing A and there's thing B, and they merge. And if it works out really well, if this new structure works, then that becomes the thing A again, that that becomes the fundamental unit. And then it sort of like gets bigger and bigger. And then that new thing will merge with another thing B. And if that works, that becomes a thing. And that life is essentially or sort of like the growing complexity of the world is essentially not necessarily a form of like, Darwinian randomness where like maybe something, there's a bunch of mutations and some of them work out well, that actually it's a little bit more ordered and structured by which new things emerge because they work out really well when they cooperate during that process of symbiosis and that that becomes the new unit of life or whatever it is. Maybe there were musicians, individuals, and then suddenly it turned out that a band could be a unit of economics or whatever and then so forth. So this idea of like, yeah, I don't know where I'm going with this, but this idea that like the symbiosis as the thing, cooperation as the thing that drives life and creativity forward, a lot of people seem to be, this seems to resonate with a lot of people.
turns.zh: 他说的一模一样：其实进化是共同进化（co-evolution），如果你去看万物的历史，世界基本上是这样浮现出来的：有个东西 A，有个东西 B，它们融合。如果结果非常好，如果这个新结构行得通，那它就又变成了那个'东西 A'，变成了那个基本单元。然后它就变得越来越大。接着那个新东西又会跟另一个'东西 B'融合。如果那个也行得通，它就又变成了一个'东西'。而生命，本质上——或者说世界日益增长的复杂性，本质上——不一定是一种达尔文式（Darwinian）的随机过程，也就是也许有一堆突变、其中一些结果不错；实际上，新事物之所以浮现，是更有序、更有结构的，因为它们在共生（symbiosis）的过程中合作得非常出色，于是那就变成了新的生命单元，或者别的什么。也许曾经有过一些音乐人、个体，然后突然间发现，一个乐队可以成为一个经济单元，或者别的什么，诸如此类。所以这个想法，就是说，对，我不知道我想说到哪儿去，但这个想法——共生才是那个关键，合作才是推动生命和创造力向前的那个东西——很多人似乎都，这似乎能引起很多人的共鸣。

turns.en: Yeah, and it's coming from a lot of different areas, whether it's economics or biology or whatever. It's coming, yeah, as a metaphor, it's kind of springing up here and there. there and you go, oh, okay, this is a real thing now.
turns.zh: 对，而且它来自很多不同的领域，不管是经济学、生物学还是别的什么。它正在，对，作为一个比喻，它正在这儿那儿冒出来。这儿那儿冒出来，然后你会想，哦，好吧，这如今是个真实存在的东西了。

turns.en: Schwanderist was the insult. You're a real Schwanderist.
turns.zh: 那句骂人的话是'Schwanderist'。'你真是个 Schwanderist。'

turns.en: That's a good one. Which sounds cutting. But the guy was right.
turns.zh: 这句挺妙。听起来很尖刻。但那个人是对的。

turns.en: It'd be unjust to his legacy.
turns.zh: 这对他的遗产来说不太公平。

turns.en: It sounds like it could be like a classic Yiddish insult.
turns.zh: 它听起来像是那种经典的意第绪语（Yiddish）骂人话。

turns.en: Doesn't it? It's like, oh, The Schwenderist.
turns.zh: 是不是？就像，哦，'那个 Schwenderist'。

turns.en: Can I ask, do you have any intuitions or a gut sense of where we should be looking for sleeping beauties today? Like particular places where maybe our biases have prevented us from seeing these old ideas.
turns.zh: 我能问一下吗，你有没有什么直觉，或者一种直觉上的感觉，觉得我们今天该去哪里寻找这些 sleeping beauties？比如某些特定的地方，也许我们的偏见妨碍了我们去看到这些古老的想法。

turns.en: If I knew that for sure, I'd be a very rich person. Yes. I'd be coming on this show for a different reason. But like you mentioned earlier, one technique seems to be kind of a pluralistic.
turns.zh: 如果我能确定那个，我早就成了非常富有的人了。对。我上这个节目也会是出于另一个理由了。但就像你之前提到的，有一种技巧似乎是一种多元的——

turns.en: Cross-disciplinary approach.
turns.zh: 跨学科（cross-disciplinary）的方法。

turns.en: Don't be in your silo. You have to be to some extent, but don't be too isolated in your silo. Along the same lines, there's the idea of how things get labeled and classified. That puts them into a box or a silo or whatever, and they can stay in there. Various kind of academics are trying to use formulas and different things to find patterns. AI might be interested. I mean, it is good at pattern identification. So you might see that in academic things where something's measurable, like citations. In science papers, if you see a little tiny uptick, if the ramp of the uptick takes a certain curve, you go, something's Da-na-na, alarm goes off. Something's happening there. But that's, again, something that is fairly easy to measure. Some of the other things are a little bit harder.
turns.zh: 别待在你的信息茧房（silo）里。某种程度上你必须待，但别在自己的筒仓里太与世隔绝。沿着同样的思路，还有关于事物如何被贴上标签、被归类的问题。那会把它们放进一个盒子、一个筒仓或者别的什么里面，然后它们就可能一直待在里面。各种各样的学者正试着用公式和不同的方法去寻找规律。AI 也许会感兴趣。我是说，它确实擅长模式识别（pattern identification）。所以你可能会在学术领域看到这一点，在那里某样东西是可衡量的，比如引用次数。在科学论文里，如果你看到一个小小的上扬，如果那个上扬的斜率呈现某种特定的曲线，你就会想，'有事了'——警报拉响。那儿正在发生什么。但那，同样，是相对容易衡量的东西。另外一些东西就稍微难衡量一点。

turns.en: Twenty-something years ago, you got into making art out of PowerPoint.
turns.zh: 二十几年前，你开始用 PowerPoint 来做艺术。

turns.en: Was the world ready at that point?
turns.zh: 那个时候世界准备好了吗？

turns.en: Or is that the sort of thing that, like, in the year 2050, like, how old was the reception to that? And would it be, like, maybe it was a little bit too early, like Moby Dick was?
turns.zh: 还是说，那属于那种，比如到了 2050 年，人们才会——那个东西当时的反响有多超前？它会不会，比如说，也许它有点太超前了，就像《Moby Dick》当年那样？

turns.en: Yeah, I did. I decided that PowerPoint would be an art medium because you can throw everything into it. You can throw type. You can throw pictures. You can throw films. You can throw sound. It's like this basket. You can throw everything in there, and it'll animate them and do all these things in a very clunky way, but whatever. So I wasn't dealing with whether it makes a good and accurate presentation. presentation or not. I was dealing with it in another way and saying, it's a creative medium. Um, and of course, a lot of people found this very funny because they have to deal with it in their daily lives. And they probably hate it.
turns.zh: 对，我做过。我当时决定，PowerPoint 会是一种艺术媒介，因为你可以把所有东西都扔进去。你可以扔进文字，可以扔进图片，可以扔进影片，可以扔进声音。它就像一个篮子。你可以把所有东西都扔进去，它会让它们动起来、做所有这些事，虽然方式很笨拙，但无所谓。所以我关注的不是它做不做得出一份好的、准确的演示文稿（presentation）。我是在用另一种方式对待它，说它是一种创作媒介。嗯，当然，很多人觉得这非常好笑，因为他们在日常生活中不得不应对它。而且他们大概很讨厌它。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: They probably, they all hate it.
turns.zh: 他们大概，他们全都讨厌它。

turns.en: Now, wait a second. I'm sure some junior analysts think that PowerPoint is indeed an art form.
turns.zh: 哎，等一下。我敢肯定有些初级分析师认为 PowerPoint 确实是一种艺术形式。

turns.en: Really? You think so?
turns.zh: 真的？你这么觉得？

turns.en: I'm being facetious.
turns.zh: 我是在开玩笑。

turns.en: Okay. Okay. I remember, uh, so I did this kind of presentation about this idea. Um, And I told, as part of it, I told kind of the history of the development of PowerPoint. And I remember doing it, doing one of these in Berkeley. And, of course, some of the guys that did it were there in the audience. They came to see what was happening. And I said, they're here, so-and-so, will you stand up? Uh-uh. They wouldn't do it. They wouldn't show themselves. I see. Yeah, it's not very loved, but I thought, oh, now you can have fun with it.
turns.zh: 好。好。我记得，呃，所以我做了这么一个关于这个想法的演示。嗯，作为其中一部分，我讲了 PowerPoint 的发展史。我记得我在 Berkeley（伯克利）做过其中一场。当然，一些当年做这个东西的人就在观众席里。他们来看看发生了什么。然后我说，他们在这儿呢，某某某，你能站起来吗？呃-呃。他们不肯。他们不愿露面。我明白。对，它不怎么受人喜爱，但我当时想，哦，现在你可以拿它来玩出点花样了。

turns.en: When you wrote the song Glass, Concrete, and Stone, by that point, did you know about Roman concrete?
turns.zh: 当你写那首歌《Glass, Concrete, and Stone》（玻璃、混凝土与石头）的时候，那时候你知道罗马混凝土的事吗？

turns.en: No, I did not. No, I did not.
turns.zh: 不，我不知道。不，我不知道。

turns.en: David Byrne, thank you so much for coming on Oblaws.
turns.zh: David Byrne，非常感谢你上 Odd Lots（节目）。

turns.en: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Tracy, that was a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 谢谢。谢谢。谢谢。Tracy，这非常有意思。

turns.en: I feel like everything he writes about in his book resonates with us both on the specific level, as in the specific things he identifies are very interesting and very us, like concrete, but also resonates with us in the sense of just finding things that other people have forgotten or ignored or looked over.
turns.zh: 我觉得他书里写的所有东西，都在两个层面上跟我们产生了共鸣：一是在具体层面上，也就是他所指出的那些具体事物非常有意思、非常'我们'，比如混凝土；二是它也跟我们共鸣，就那种去发现别人已经遗忘、忽视或略过的东西这件事本身。

turns.en: Absolutely. I mean, the virality of ideas is something that we've talked about before. It's funny to think I never thought we'd be talking to David Byrne about concrete. And I had the song going through my head during the conversation. You may find yourself on a beautiful podcast. Yeah. In a random part of the world, talking about concrete.
turns.zh: 绝对的。我是说，想法的病毒式传播（virality）是我们以前就聊过的话题。有意思的是，我从没想过我们会跟 David Byrne 聊混凝土。而且对话期间那首歌一直在我脑子里转。'You may find yourself'（你可能会发现自己）在一档美妙的播客上。对。在世界的某个角落，聊着混凝土。

turns.en: With David Byrne.
turns.zh: 和 David Byrne 一起。

turns.en: We should have gotten into this. But he talks a little bit about the power structures that restrain good ideas from taking hold. And it kind of comes up in the background of something like concrete, where there are vested interests who maybe don't want to use a particular concrete formula because they base their entire business on Portland concrete. It comes up in his chapter about solar panels, where it turns out there was an early iteration of solar panels that could have been groundbreaking for the world, but obviously there were vested interests in oil and things like that. And so there are these power structures that restrain a lot of good ideas from taking hold. I do think his conclusions, the sort of cross-disciplinary approach to resurfacing some of this stuff is really interesting and harder than it seems. This is almost a fundamental question when it comes to Information science, because the tendency of human beings is to want to neatly categorize everything, taxonomize everything, slot everything into neat little categories. Expertise is often very siloed. It's hard to become a generalist or it's hard to become a good generalist. And so really figuring out how to bring those different disciplines or approaches together, like that seems to be the real challenge here. Like why aren't contractors reading, you know, like ancient Roman architectural texts?
turns.zh: 我们本该聊聊这个的。但他稍微谈到了那些阻碍好想法扎根的权力结构（power structures）。这在混凝土这类事情的背景里就有体现：有一些既得利益者（vested interests），他们也许不想用某种特定的混凝土配方，因为他们的整个生意都建立在 Portland concrete（波特兰混凝土）之上。这在他讲太阳能板（solar panels）的那一章里也出现了，结果发现，太阳能板早期有一个版本，本可以对全世界具有开创性意义，但显然石油等领域存在既得利益。所以就有这么一些权力结构，阻碍了很多好想法扎根。我确实认为他的结论——那种用跨学科的方法来重新浮现其中一些东西——真的很有意思，而且比看上去更难。这在信息科学（information science）里几乎是个根本性的问题，因为人类的天性就是想把一切都整齐地归类、给一切建立分类学（taxonomize）、把一切都塞进整齐的小格子里。专业知识往往是非常筒仓化（siloed）的。要成为一个通才（generalist）、或者成为一个好的通才，是很难的。所以真正搞清楚如何把那些不同的学科或方法整合到一起，似乎才是这里真正的挑战。就像，为什么承包商不去读那些古罗马的建筑文本呢？
